h1: Admiral hops for high alpha bittering from England
title: Admiral Hops for High Alpha Bittering | Craft Beer School
desc: Admiral hops explained: England's high alpha bittering variety, its typical analysis, how much to use and the beers where its resinous orange note fits.
teaser: Admiral packs 13 to 16% alpha into an English hop. That means a lot of bitterness from very few pellets.
standfirst: Admiral is the strongest of the traditional English bittering hops. It gives clean, firm bitterness with a resinous orange edge. Here is what it does and how to dose it without overshooting.
sections: England's answer to the high alpha varieties

Admiral was bred in England at Wye and released in the late 1990s. English growers wanted a home grown hop that could compete on bitterness per kilo with the high alpha varieties coming out of the United States and Germany. Admiral delivered. Alpha acid usually lands between 13 and 16%, close to Warrior and Magnum territory.

It is still recognisably English in flavour. Descriptions mention resin, orange peel, citrus and herbal notes. Used as a bittering hop at 60 minutes, most of that aroma boils away and what stays is a firm, fairly clean bitterness.
What 15% alpha does to your recipe

High alpha means small weights. For a 20 litre batch at 40 IBU with one 60 minute addition and about 25% utilisation:

grams = 40 x 20 / (0.15 x 0.25 x 1,000) = about 21 g.

On a 1,000 litre brewhouse at 28% utilisation, the same 40 IBU takes about 950 g of Admiral against roughly 2,850 g of a 5% Golding. That is a real saving in hop cost and a much smaller trub cone. It also means a weighing error matters more. A 50 g slip on a 950 g addition is 2 IBU. On a homebrew scale, a 3 g slip is nearly 6 IBU.

The floor detail: weigh Admiral on a scale that reads to the gram, not on the platform scale you use for malt bags. A platform scale with 50 g steps is fine for a 250 kg grist. It is not fine for a hop addition where every 25 g is a noticeable change in bitterness.

Check the lot alpha before every brew too. All hops lose alpha acid with time, heat and oxygen, so buy lots you will finish within the season and keep them frozen below 0 °C in sealed packs. Our guide on English hops covers storage across the family.
Where it fits and where it does not

Admiral suits big English beers that need a lot of bitterness under a lot of malt:

  • English IPAs at 45 to 60 IBU.
  • Strong bitters and ESBs.
  • Imperial stouts and barley wines, where the gravity cuts utilisation and you need high alpha to reach 60 IBU or more.

It is less useful in a 3.5% mild, where the total bitterness is so low that a few grams of Admiral is all you need and Fuggle would give better character for the same IBU. It is also not the hop for a delicate pale lager. A cleaner hop such as Magnum does that job better.

Some brewers use Admiral late in the boil or in the whirlpool for its orange and resin notes. It can work in a modern English pale ale alongside fruitier varieties such as Jester. Start small: 1 to 2 g per litre in the whirlpool at 80 °C is enough to judge it.

As a dry hop it is uncommon. The high alpha and modest oil content mean you add bitterness compounds and vegetal matter for limited aroma gain. Most brewers spend their dry hop budget on aroma varieties.
A worked Admiral recipe for a strong bitter

Here is a simple 20 litre strong bitter at about OG 1.052 to show how little Admiral you need:

  • Maris Otter pale malt 4.3 kg (90%).
  • Crystal malt around 120 EBC 0.38 kg (8%).
  • Torrefied wheat 0.1 kg (2%).
  • Admiral at 15% alpha, 60 minutes: about 18 g for 34 IBU.
  • Goldings at 5%, 10 minutes: 20 g for a further 4 to 5 IBU, plus aroma.

Ferment with an English ale yeast at 18 to 20 °C. The Admiral sets the backbone. The Goldings give the beer its English accent. Swap the Admiral for Target and you will need about 23 g at 12% for the same bitterness.

English hops reach India by sea or air, then wait in customs, then travel by road. Every warm day on that route costs alpha acid. For a high alpha hop bought for its bitterness, that loss is money. Ask your supplier for the harvest year and the date of the analysis. A lot analysed six months ago and held warm will test lower now.

If you can, run your own check: brew a small standard batch and send it for an IBU test, or compare a trusted recipe's taste against your memory of earlier batches. It is crude. It still beats trusting a number printed at a farm in Kent half a year ago.

Target is the nearest English swap, with more herbal pungency. Challenger works with a little more weight. Outside England, Magnum, Warrior or Bravo can replace it for bittering. Our guides on Warrior and Herkules compare them.

When you swap, recalculate from alpha acid and taste the result. The IBU number will match. The perceived bitterness may not, because oil content and cohumulone shift how harsh or smooth it feels on the palate.
faqs: How much alpha acid does Admiral have?
Admiral typically tests between 13 and 16% alpha acid, which makes it one of the highest alpha English varieties.
Is Admiral a good aroma hop?
It is mainly a bittering hop. Late additions give resin and orange notes, but most brewers keep their aroma budget for oilier varieties.
What is a good substitute for Admiral?
Target or Challenger from England, or Magnum, Warrior or Bravo for clean bittering. Scale the weight by alpha acid.
